correctness.rationale: For the integer squared Padovan recurrence the explicit monic annihilator Q has Q(1)=-1, so vanishing of every window modulo any integer is equivalent to its length being a squared-sequence period. The six initial windows determine the full gcd. Integer matrices show A^7=I mod 2, A^14=I+4B with B_01=1 mod 2, and A^13=I+3C with C v_2 nonzero mod 3. Binomial lifting yields both full prime-power period ladders, including separate small-precision cases and nonperiod witnesses. CHECKS.txt records an independently executed 720-case two-prime GCD comparison and 14 complete modular periods; those are finite corroborations, not used to prove infinite quantifiers.

originality.rationale: The first-public 2021 Guyer–Mbirika source (arXiv:2104.12262v1) is limited to unsquared second-order Gibonacci sums; a Padovan finite-group paper is about unsquared modular recurrence. Closest indexed period result concerns primitive Padovan orbit state periods, not Padovan squares, and closest squared-window gcds concern Jacobsthal, Pell, or Tribonacci rather than the claimed exact factors. Neither prior result as inspected implies the all-length specific local period ladders; binary shortening and ternary sharp witness require new analysis. Inaccessible full texts and potential implicit symmetric-square treatments remain disclosed.
residual_risks: Full GitHub texts of relevant published summaries were inaccessible; comparisons at those sources are based on actual summaries and not full-document absence claims.
A stronger or unindexed general symmetric-square recurrence period theorem may imply this specialization without stating Padovan.
The existing record collection and searched bibliographic databases are not proofs of novelty.

value.rationale: The all-window gcd is a natural arithmetic object studied for second-order unsquared recurrences. For the first non-Fibonacci classical third-order recurrence, the result identifies exact local factors for every k at two distinct primes and detects an unusual strict period-halving at all higher powers of two, while powers of three have unreduced lifts. These precise prime-power criteria answer meaningful local divisibility questions without computing window sums; no general beyond-the-scope theorem is needed.
